3) Structured output / tool-calling: best practices for schema enforcement and validation.
4) Embeddings / reranker: indexing cadence and similarity thresholds.
5) Prompt governance: versioning, prompt injection mitigations, and red-team suggestions.

Thanks Marissa \u0014 adding the technical details below per our discussion. This is a short reference that we can expand into a design doc if you'd like.

1) SDK setup & auth- Server-side integration recommended: use Redwood service tokens bound to a project-level role.
- Example flow: ACME backend calls Redwood over TLS with a scoped service token (rotate via your KMS).
- SDKs (Go/Python/Node) provide automatic retry/backoff and streaming helpers. See attached quickstart and sample env vars.

2) Routing & model variants- Use policy-based routing: low-latency tier (gptx-8-fast) for interactive UI, cost tier (gptx-8-cost) for background summarization.
- Autoscaling: configure burst capacity + regional fallback (us-east -> us-west) for outages.

3) Structured output & tool-calling- Use JSON-schema-enforced structured output with function/tool calling for CRM operations.
- Recommendation: validate schema client-side and server-side; include field-level type checks to avoid prompt-injection-induced schema changes.

4) Embeddings / reranker- Periodic reindex (nightly) for product catalog; incremental updates for new records.
- Reranker as a lightweight second-stage model to reorder beam results; keep logging for drift detection.

5) Prompt templates & governance- Version your prompt templates in source control (example branch: prompts/v1.0).
- Add CI checks to run a small set of unit prompts (sanity + adversarial) against a staging model before merge.
- For prompt injection mitigation: prefer structured prompts with explicit schema + guardrails, sanitize user-controlled fields, and prefer server-side templating over client-side concatenation.

If helpful, I can sketch a minimal PoC repo with example CI checks and prompt-versioning hooks.

Hi Jordan / Priya / SecOps \u0014 following up with a concrete proposal that maps to your questions. TL;DR: we recommend a combined dev-time + inference-time approach with CI, versioning, runtime guards, and periodic red-team exercises.

Proposed prompt governance workflow
1) Source control + tagging: store canonical prompt templates in your repo (prompts/), tag releases (v1.0, v1.1) and link each deployment to a prompt hash.
2) CI checks: on PR, run unit prompts (happy path, edge cases, adversarial injections) against a staging model. Fail the pipeline on schema drift or unsafe outputs.
3) Staging hold & approvals: require at least one security review for changes labeled security-impacting.
4) Runtime metadata & auditing: include prompt version id in every call (x-prompt-version header) and persist with logs/trace for auditing.

Prompt injection mitigations (dev-time vs inference-time)- Dev-time: template hardening, sanitize user inputs, use parameterized placeholders rather than concatenation, run adversarial test suite in CI.
- Inference-time: enforce output schema validation, server-side post-processing to reject/repair outputs that don't match schema, use tool-calling only after schema validation. Also implement rate limits on content-generation endpoints.

Red-team & regression testing- Quarterly red-team runs: use both automated adversarial generation and human testers to probe for injection, data leaks, and hallucination scenarios.
- Coverage metrics: percentage of template lines exercised, attack vectors attempted, and escape-success rate.

Architecture notes on server vs client- Server-side only: service tokens, token rotation, prompt signing (if used), embeddings write operations, indexing jobs.
- Client-side: UI SDK for streaming and display, but never embed service-level tokens in client builds.

We attached a short checklist that your security team can use as a starting point. Happy to walk Priya/SecOps through it in a 30m session.
